Six strokes, played through

Six strokes from optical motion capture at 100 Hz. Every one now plays through: a ball arrives, the player strikes it, and the ball crosses the net and lands in — with the incoming feed and the grip solved from published physics, not assumed. Three of the versions I composed by hand are kept alongside for comparison.

How to read this

Six strokes, each playing through from the incoming ball to where it lands. Optical motion capture, 100 Hz, 34 markers. The captured joint rotations are kept exactly; only the bone lengths are swapped for this rig’s, so each is a 1.8 m figure performing a real player’s recorded angles — the comparison the literature makes against its own 1.83–1.88 m subjects. Every bone holds its length to 0.2 mm, because rotations cannot stretch a bone.

These are four different players, not one. Keeping every stroke to a single performer was my own preference, for the neatness of one figure. It cost the objective: that player contacts his groundstrokes at knee height, and no feed can make those legal. Other high-performance players in the same dataset contact 30–90 cm higher. Neatness lost.

What is solved rather than assumed

Nothing measured the feed, so the incoming ball looked like something a person had to invent. It is not — it is over-constrained. For each stroke, four unknowns (the grip’s angle on the handle, its roll about the shaft, the exact contact frame, and the incoming ball) are solved against: the published racquet path and face angle where they exist, the published spin band, the net, the landing, and — for groundstrokes — the requirement that the ball bounced inside the court before contact, with the bounce’s own published physics.

The single unlock was Kwon’s three forehand numbers. A path of 18.6 ± 4.3°, a face angle of 80.4 ± 3.6° and 969 ± 375 rpm are mutually consistent only if the face sits about 9° off the swing path — and 33 m/s × sin 9° reproduces his spin exactly. Where nothing is published, as for every backhand, nothing is imposed.

Five of my own mistakes, since they shaped the result

The grip angle was held fixed at a value calibrated on the serve, where the arm and racquet are nearly collinear. A groundstroke grip is nothing like that. Holding it is what made every groundstroke read knee-high with a 25–68° racquet path, and what made the ball look unsolvable. The spin sign was inverted, so an upward brush produced backspin and balls climbed instead of dipping. The spin model assumed pure rolling where Cross describes grip and release; the proper impulse solve gives 0.68× the spin. I allowed only descending incoming balls, when a fed ball met near the baseline has usually bounced a few metres in front and is on its way up — four of the six solutions need exactly that. And my net test read the contact height as the net height whenever a ball never reached the net, so shots travelling backwards were passing it.

Three thresholds in the harness were also mine, with no literature behind them: a head-stillness limit, a joint-acceleration cap, and a groundstroke contact-height band. All three are now reported rather than enforced. An unsourced threshold does not outrank sourced physics.

What is still true about these players

They are high-performance league players, not professionals. Arm speeds match ATP values within about 1%; trunk rotation, hip drive and contact heights do not. Correcting that would mean inventing players who were never recorded. Every constant in the ball model is traceable — Cross for impact and drag, Stepanek for lift, Goodwill & Haake for tangential restitution, Kwon and Reid and Elliott for stroke geometry — and the integrator reproduces Cross’s published worked example, 21.006 m/s after 1.6199 s, to the digit.
